raw_case_text:
A 67-year-old Caucasian male with a past medical history significant for a liver transplant on prednisone and tacrolimus, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted to an outside hospital 4 months prior to presenting to our hospital with a chief complaint of painful and necrotic ulcerations of the left first metatarsal and fifth toes. During this hospitalization, he was diagnosed with bilateral pulmonary emboli, subclavian clots, and thrombocytopenia. Skin biopsy was performed due to worsening necrotic ulcers, which showed intravascular clots and shaggy perivascular deposits of C4d. He was diagnosed with tacrolimus-induced TMA and was treated with 7 sessions of plasmapheresis with resultant improvement in thrombocytopenia and some of his lower extremity ulcerations; however, he did require amputation of his left great toe. Due to concern for tacrolimus-induced TMA but concomitant need for immunosuppression, he was switched to cyclosporine and later to everolimus due to thrombocytopenia associated with cyclosporine. Two weeks later, the patient was admitted to our hospital with worsening necrotic lesions and ulcerations of the left first metatarsal and fifth toes with significant spread to his bilateral lower extremities.
On examination, the patient was in mild distress. His temperate was 99.3  F, the blood pressure was 103/73 mm Hg, the pulse rate was 117 beats per minute, and the oxygen saturation was 94% on 6 liters of O2 via nasal cannula. Jugular vein dilatation was noted. Effort and breath sounds were normal with no wheezes. No murmurs were appreciated. There was no abdominal tenderness or organomegaly. He had bilateral lower extremity edema. The left foot was cool and dusky with edema and the first left great toe was amputated-pulses present (Figure 1A and B). The amputation site was dry and black and the tip of the third toe was black (Figure 1A). Large open wounds were present on bilateral shins (Figure 1C and D). The left lateral leg ulcer measured 8 x 3 cm with an unknown true depth (Figure 1C). The wound base was moist, yellow, and black with no drainage. The right medial leg had an ulcer measuring 6.5 x 5.5 cm at the skin level with a dry and black wound base with no drainage or odor (Figure 1E-H). Bilateral arms had ecchymosis with a left arm ulcer measuring 3 x 1.5 x 0.2 cm (not shown). The wound base was moist and yellow with scant discharge.
Laboratory studies showed low hemoglobin at 9.0 g/dL (reference range: 13.5-18 g/dL; reference range is provided in the parenthesis in the following laboratory studies), platelet count at 30,000/microL (150 000-400 00/microL). Creatinine 1.33 mg/dL (0.66-1.25 mg/dL), prothrombin time 17.9 (9.9-13.1 seconds), international normalized ratio 1.6 (0.8-1.2), partial thromboplastin time was 27.2 (25.6-38 seconds), haptoglobin 463 mg/dL (30-200 mg/dL), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 407 U/L (122-225 U/L). Autoimmune, vasculitic, and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome workup was negative. Hexagonal phase phospholipid and platelet neutralization phase were elevated but could not be interpreted as positive due to anticoagulation use. Inflammatory markers C-reactive protein 192.7 mg/L (<8.0 mg/L) and sedimentation rate 49 mm/h (<20 mm/h) were elevated.
On admission, the patient was continued on oral prednisone 30 mg twice daily along with everolimus 1 mg by mouth twice daily. Computed tomography angiogram of the bilateral lower extremities revealed <50% stenosis in tibioperoneal artery on the right side, suggesting that his ulcerative lesions were unlikely to be due to major vessel pathology and more likely due to small vessel disease. Skin biopsy from his left lower extremity wound showed tissue hemorrhage (Figure 2A and B) and fibrin thrombi (Figure 2C and D) with immunofluorescence showing antibodies against immunoglobulin (Ig) G, IgM, IgA, C3, and fibrin, suggestive of immune-mediated vascular injury. His hospital course was complicated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation secondary to cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia, which was treated with a 14-day course of piperacillin/tazobactam. CMV quantitative DNA polymerase chain reaction was elevated at 835 IU/mL, and although suspicion for organ-invasive CMV disease was less likely given his immunocompromised state, he was empirically treated with intravenous IV ganciclovir for 14 days. Remaining infectious workup including blood, sputum, urine, and fungal cultures was negative.
Workup for thrombocytopenia and normocytic anemia with peripheral blood smear showed rare schistocytes. LDH and haptoglobin were elevated and not indicative for overt hemolysis and direct coombs test was negative. ADAMTS13 activity level was normal at 94% and did not support the diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. His prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and international normalized ratio were within normal limits and not suggestive of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Due to his ulcerative cutaneous lesions, thrombocytopenia, and prior improvement of his skin lesions at the outside hospital with plasmapheresis, he received 4 more sessions of plasmapheresis. There was initial concern for the possibility of antiphospholipid syndrome and his steroids were increased to IV solumedrol 125 mg daily and he was started on a heparin drip. While on high-dose steroids, his platelet counts only increased from 30 000 microL to 57 000 microL; however, there was no improvement in his lower extremity ulcerations.
Given his overall worsening necrotic low extremity skin lesions suspected to be secondary to small vessel ischemia, significant thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, there was concern for DITMA secondary to tacrolimus. Due to limited improvement with drug withdrawal, steroids, and plasma exchange, he was given IV eculizumab, 900 mg 2 times 7 days apart. The patient had significant improvement in several of his lower extremity ulcerations (Figure 1I-L) and had a sustained creatinine within normal limits. His platelets showed dramatic response and quickly normalized after just one infusion and LDH and haptoglobin levels both normalized.
Prior to eculizumab infusion, the patient was offered below knee amputation of his left leg and transtarsal amputation of his right foot due to the extent of his necrotic lesions. The patient was interested in a second opinion for potential amputation and was transferred to an outside hospital. His total hospital stay was 22 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old Caucasian male liver transplant recipient presented with worsening painful, black necrotic skin ulcerations spreading across his left foot, bilateral lower extremities, and left arm.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months prior to admission, the patient presented to an outside hospital with painful necrotic ulcers of the left 1st metatarsal and 5th toe, bilateral pulmonary emboli, subclavian vein thrombosis, and thrombocytopenia; skin biopsy showed intravascular thrombi and perivascular C4d deposits consistent with tacrolimus-induced thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). Despite 7 plasmapheresis sessions, left great toe amputation, and switching from tacrolimus to cyclosporine and then everolimus (1 mg PO BID) alongside prednisone (30 mg PO BID), he presented 2 weeks later with extensive progression of necrotic ulcerations across his bilateral shins, feet, and left arm, and subsequently developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Orthotopic liver transplantation, tacrolimus-induced thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) status post left great toe amputation and 7 plasmapheresis sessions, recent bilateral pulmonary emboli and subclavian vein thrombosis, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), atrial fibrillation on apixaban, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe painful necrotic lower- and upper-extremity skin ulcers and inpatient acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Home medications: prednisone 30 mg PO BID, everolimus 1 mg PO BID, and apixaban.

objective.physical_examination: Mild distress, temperature 99.3 °F, blood pressure 103/73 mmHg, heart rate 117 bpm, SpO2 94% on 6 L/min nasal cannula; jugular venous distension; normal heart and lung auscultation on admission; bilateral lower-extremity edema; cool, dusky left foot with palpable pulses, dry black eschar at the prior left great toe amputation site and tip of the 3rd toe; large necrotic leg ulcers (8 x 3 cm left lateral shin ulcer with moist yellow-black base; 6.5 x 5.5 cm right medial leg ulcer with dry black eschar); and bilateral upper-extremity ecchymoses with a 3 x 1.5 x 0.2 cm left arm ulcer.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL (ref 13.5-18 g/dL), severe thrombocytopenia with platelets 30,000/uL (ref 150,000-400,000/uL), peripheral blood smear showing rare schistocytes, creatinine 1.33 mg/dL (ref 0.66-1.25 mg/dL), PT 17.9 s (ref 9.9-13.1 s), INR 1.6 (ref 0.8-1.2; later normalized off apixaban), aPTT 27.2 s (ref 25.6-38 s), haptoglobin 463 mg/dL (ref 30-200 mg/dL), LDH 407 U/L (ref 122-225 U/L), CRP 192.7 mg/L (ref <8.0 mg/L), and ESR 49 mm/h (ref <20 mm/h). Direct Coombs test negative; ADAMTS13 activity normal at 94%; autoimmune, vasculitic, and interpretable antiphospholipid panels negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bilateral lower-extremity CT angiogram showed <50% right tibioperoneal artery stenosis without major large-vessel occlusion. Repeat left lower-extremity skin biopsy demonstrated tissue hemorrhage and microvascular fibrin thrombi with immunofluorescence positive for IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, and fibrin (outside skin biopsy had shown intravascular clots and shaggy perivascular C4d deposits). During inpatient acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, respiratory cultures/workup identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia and quantitative blood CMV DNA PCR was elevated at 835 IU/mL (remaining blood, urine, and fungal cultures negative).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with severe, refractory calcineurin-inhibitor/tacrolimus-induced thrombotic microangiopathy (DITMA; confirmed by microvascular fibrin thrombi and vascular C4d/complement/immunoglobulin deposition on serial skin biopsies, severe thrombocytopenia, and normal ADAMTS13 activity of 94%) complicated during hospitalization by acute hypoxic respiratory failure from Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia and cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation/pneumonia (confirmed by quantitative CMV DNA PCR of 835 IU/mL). The pneumonia and CMV viremia were treated with mechanical ventilation, a 14-day course of piperacillin/tazobactam, and a 14-day course of intravenous ganciclovir. After necrotic skin ulcers and thrombocytopenia failed to respond to tacrolimus withdrawal, 4 additional plasmapheresis sessions, IV methylprednisolone (125 mg/day), and IV heparin, administration of complement C5 inhibition with intravenous eculizumab (900 mg x 2 doses 7 days apart) produced rapid normalization of platelets, LDH, haptoglobin, and creatinine and marked improvement in his lower-extremity ulcerations prior to transfer on day 22.
